samples.text:
In many cities today, old factories and warehouses are being changed into expensive flats, shops and cafes. I think this is mostly a positive development, although it also has some negative effects on local people.

Firstly, redevelopment makes the city more beautiful and safer. Old industrial areas are often empty and dirty, and sometimes they become dangerous places at night. When these buildings are repaired and turned into apartments and cafes, the area become more lively and attractive. People start to walk there, go shopping and meet friends, so the whole neighbourhood improve.

Secondly, these projects are good for the economy. Building new apartments and shops create many jobs, both during the construction and after that, in the cafes and stores. The city government also receive more money from taxes, which it can spend on public services like schools and transport. In addition, using old buildings is better than building on green land outside the city.

On the other hand, there is a big problem, which is that the new apartments are very expensive. Local people who lived near the old factories often cannot afford the higher rent, so they have to move to another area. This is unfair, because they lived there for many years and they lose their community.

In conclusion, I believe that turning old industrial areas into apartments, shops and cafes is a positive development because it improves the city and the economy. However, the government should make sure that some cheaper homes are also built, so local people can stay in their area.
samples.why: Clear position · relevant main ideas with limited extension · mechanical sequencing (Firstly, Secondly, On the other hand) · adequate vocabulary · recurring subject-verb agreement errors that do not obscure meaning.

samples.text:
Across many cities, abandoned factories, docks and warehouses are being converted into luxury flats, boutiques and coffee shops. While such regeneration brings visible improvements, I believe that in its current form it is more of a negative development than a positive one, mainly because of its effect on existing residents.

Admittedly, there are clear benefits. Derelict industrial sites can be unsightly and even unsafe, and restoring them brings life back to neglected parts of a city. Converting existing buildings is also more sustainable than building on the countryside, and new businesses create jobs and generate tax revenue for local authorities. In some cases, historic industrial architecture is preserved that might otherwise have been demolished.

However, these benefits are not shared equally. As an area becomes fashionable, property prices and rents rise sharply, and long-term residents, who are often working-class families, are gradually priced out. The people who lived through the area's decline are therefore frequently unable to enjoy its revival. The small, affordable shops that served them are replaced by expensive cafes that cater mainly for newcomers and visitors.

Furthermore, this process can weaken the social fabric of a city. Established communities, with their networks of neighbours, schools and local organisations, are broken up when families are forced to move to cheaper districts further from the centre. Over time, cities risk becoming divided into wealthy inner areas and poorer outer suburbs, which increase inequality and commuting times for those with the lowest incomes.

In conclusion, although redeveloping old industrial areas improves the appearance and economy of cities, the displacement of local communities is too high a price to pay. Unless regeneration schemes include a significant share of affordable housing, I regard this trend as largely negative.
samples.why: Clear negative position with benefits acknowledged · ideas extended and linked logically · clear central topic per paragraph · good collocations (priced out, social fabric) · largely accurate with an occasional agreement slip.

samples.text:
In cities around the world, the disused factories and warehouses of a former industrial age are being reborn as upmarket apartments, independent boutiques and artisan cafes. This transformation is often celebrated as urban renewal, and in many respects it is. On balance, however, I believe its benefits are real but narrowly distributed, which makes it, as currently practised, a largely negative development.

The case for regeneration is by no means weak. Vacant industrial land tends to attract crime and dereliction, and bringing it back into use can revitalise surrounding streets. Reusing existing structures is also considerably more sustainable than expanding into greenfield sites, and it can preserve architecture that gives a city its distinctive character. Local authorities, meanwhile, benefit from higher tax receipts and new employment.

The difficulty lies in who ultimately enjoys these gains. Once a former industrial district acquires a reputation as fashionable, land values rise and rents follow. Long-standing residents, frequently on modest incomes, find themselves unable to remain in neighbourhoods they have lived in for decades, and the hardware shops and inexpensive cafes they relied upon give way to businesses aimed at a more affluent clientele. What is presented as improvement for an area can thus amount to the replacement of one population by another.

The wider consequences are equally concerning. When displaced families relocate to peripheral suburbs, they lose not only their homes but also the informal support networks that sustain communities, while facing longer and more expensive journeys to work. Repeated across a city, this pattern produces a polarised urban landscape in which the centre becomes the preserve of the wealthy.

In conclusion, converting industrial land into expensive housing and leisure spaces undoubtedly revitalises the physical fabric of cities, but it too often does so at the expense of the people who already live there. Unless such projects are required to include genuinely affordable homes, the trend should be viewed as more harmful than beneficial.
samples.why: Sophisticated, clearly reasoned negative judgement · opposing view given due weight · ideas fully extended · cohesion managed effortlessly · wide, precise vocabulary (polarised, clientele) · wide range of accurate structures.
